extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and historians interested in history of mathematics and scientific priority disputes
extracted.subtask_description: A historical analysis of the Leibniz–Newton controversy over who first invented calculus, describing the evidence, contemporary priority-fixing practices, accusations, committee findings, and historiographical interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific priority mechanisms (17th century)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods used to establish priority included anagrams, sealed envelopes placed in a safe place, correspondence with other scientists, or a private message; letters to the founder of the French Academy of Sciences (Marin Mersenne) or to the secretary of the Royal Society (Henry Oldenburg) had essentially the status of a published article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These acted as time-stamps proving knowledge at a given date. When evaluating claims, treat contemporaneous sealed communications and formal letters to academies as strong contemporaneous evidence of priority. Anti-pattern: ignoring these informal but accepted time-stamping methods and relying only on later printed publication dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority via publication in a valuable context
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an idea was subsequently published 'in conjunction with its use in a particularly valuable context', that publication might take priority over an earlier discoverer's work which had no obvious application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess not only first occurrence of an idea but whether the later publication demonstrated important use or application; a later, more influential publication can supersede earlier, obscure statements. Scoring note: weight significance and impact of application when judging who 'won' priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel invention vs mere improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician's claim could be undermined by counter-claims that he had not truly invented an idea, but merely improved on someone else's idea—an improvement that required little skill and was based on facts that were already known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish true novelty from incremental improvements; evaluate the skill and conceptual leap required. Anti-pattern: treating any refinement as equivalent to original invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for Leibniz's claim of independent invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that Leibniz invented calculus independently rests on that Leibniz: (1) Published a description of his method some years before Newton printed anything on fluxions, (2) Always alluded to the discovery as being his own invention, (3) Enjoyed the strong presumption that he acted in good faith, (4) Demonstrated in his private papers his development of the ideas of calculus in a manner independent of the path taken by Newton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Leibniz's claim, check published dates, consistent public claims of originality, the presence of private developmental notes predating exposure to others' work, and contemporaneous goodwill or lack of suspicious behavior. Example evidence: Leibniz's 1684 paper and private notebooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to rebut independent invention (accusation of plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebut Leibniz's case it was sufficient (as framed by detractors) to show that he: (1) Saw some of Newton's papers on the subject in or before 1675 or at least 1677, and (2) Obtained the fundamental ideas of calculus from those papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on establishing access plus use: documentary proof that the accused saw the earlier manuscripts or copies, and demonstrable derivation of key ideas. Anti-pattern: relying on circumstantial similarity without proof of access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of private papers and notebooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Private papers that demonstrate the development of ideas (for example, Leibniz's private notebooks showing differentials) are key evidence for independent invention; likewise, discovery of extracts in Leibniz's handwriting from Newton's De Analysi raises questions about timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat original drafts, dated notes, and manuscript extracts as high-value evidence for chronology and independence; verify dates and provenance (e.g., Gerhardt's discovery of Newton extracts in Leibniz's manuscripts). Anti-pattern: accepting undated or altered notes without provenance checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of bad faith or manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of bad faith includes back-dating and changing fundamentals of 'original' notes, and publishing anonymous slanders or dishonesty in claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing credibility, look for alterations to records, inconsistent chronology, or covert attacks. Such indicators reduce the presumption of good faith and lower credibility of priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and bias of adjudicating bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society committee that judged the dispute never asked Leibniz to give his version of events; the report (Commercium Epistolicum) was written and published as 'Commercium Epistolicum' by Newton early in 1713, indicating bias in procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether investigative bodies solicited testimony from all parties and whether reports were authored impartially. Anti-pattern: accepting committee findings without examining procedural fairness or conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notational and methodological differences as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton employed fluxions and geometric forms while Leibniz used differentials; their methods were described as either 'profoundly different' or 'translatable' — the presence of different notation and approaches is used to argue both independence and equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether differences in notation reflect genuinely distinct conceptual approaches or merely different formalizations of the same underlying method. Example: Newton's fluxions (derivative-first approach) vs Leibniz's integral/summation perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual influence and shared developments
rubrics_metrics.description: Both men had some knowledge of the other's methods and 'worked together' on certain aspects (e.g., power series), and correspondence (e.g., letter to Henry Oldenburg dated 24 October 1676) shows exchange of methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging independence, consider documented interactions, shared collaborators, and correspondence that could transmit ideas. Evidence of collaboration weakens strict independent-invention claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical manuscript copies and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a copy of Newton's manuscript in Leibniz's handwriting (Gerhardt's 1849 finding) is treated as significant evidence about possible access to Newton's work and about when extracts were made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify provenance and dating of manuscript copies; distinguish between copies made from earlier circulation (e.g., copies shown by intermediaries) and copies made from printed editions. Provenance increases evidentiary weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer competition and problem-solving as demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical competitions (e.g., the calculus of variations problem organized by Johann Bernoulli) served as tests of the power and generality of competing methods; Leibniz's more general published solution was taken as a formal win.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contemporaneous problem competitions and judged outcomes as evidence of the comparative strength and originality of methods. Anti-pattern: ignoring competitive outcomes in favor of purely documentary chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of publication versus timing of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton began work earlier (e.g., 1666 manuscripts) but did not publish fluxional notation until 1693 (partly) and 1704 (in full), whereas Leibniz published in 1684; thus timing of publication and timing of private discovery can diverge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish documented dates of discovery (manuscripts, dated notes) from dates of publication. In evaluating priority, treat both types of evidence, but require clear provenance for private discovery claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of good faith and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Leibniz 'enjoyed the strong presumption that he acted in good faith' and contemporaneous assessments of character influence how claims were received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor contemporaneous reputation and prior conduct into assessment of claims, but corroborate with documentary evidence; don't let reputation alone override material proof.
